title: Clem's background; John Pendleton and Joe Oliver's limits
summary: Clem's name and origins; Oliver recommended trombonist John Pendleton for a St. Charles dance job.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: Boy, how was Clem's name spelled, the last name? Was it C or K? C.

Ed Waugh Clem. They call him Ed Waugh. He came from out around, uh, Paunchetour. I believe that is his home out in Paunchetour. He came from out there, yeah. He thought his daddy had a, had a sort of a farm out there, you know?
Talked sort of Creole? Ed Waugh?

Well, he didn't, he didn't talk, he never talked in broken, you know, Creole, but he was from, you know, from that home out there, you see? His old daddy used to talk in broken English like that, you know? But not him, cause he practically came, he must have came here when he was young, you know? He was a good trumpet player. He had plenty, plenty of work out there in the country, everything given. Well, there's another trumpet player, Pendleton. That, uh, you talking about John Pendleton. Yeah, did he? Well, he was a trombone player. Oh, trombone.
But he could play trumpet. I never knew, if somebody told, mention the name of other, just, you knew what he was

about. Yeah, yeah, yeah, I tell ya, I tell ya, he was about, he played trumpet before Joe. I mean, he could play dance music. John Pendleton, he lived uptown, way uptown, too, on, I think he lived up on Pendleton Street. He lived up there. Way uptown. Yeah, yeah. And, uh, Joe Oliver had a repair shoe shop uptown. That's, he started, he had, you know, one of the little repair shoe shops. Well, Joe was playing, uh, brass band music. He could play the trumpet, but he couldn't play nothing but, uh, brass band. You know, like these brass bands now? Yeah. Yeah. Parade music. That's all he could play. I went to high, and I had them times, I was getting plenty of work. See, all them big rich people up on St. Charles Street, they had my name and address, and they always, when they were on a good band or something like that, they'd, you know, get in touch with me, you know. Then I'd have to do a scrap up to men who'd go up there and play, you know. Yeah. I would know some of my band a whole lot of times. They'd say, all good men, you know, go up there and play. So, I'd get a job, I needed a trumpet player, and I studied it by Joe Oliver, and I'd run up there to hire him, and he told me he couldn't play no dance music, because this was going to be a big dance in the house, you know, uptown, St. Charles Street. But he said, I'll introduce you to John Pantone. He lived right about three blocks from here, he said, and told me the right way to find him at. He said he's a trombone player, but he can play trumpet. And I think he'll do, because he know more about that dance music than I do. I went around there, John Pantone, took the job, and went to come on with me and went to play it. He blowed the trombone. So, in fact, the cornet, you know, he wasn't such a hot man, but he could play, you know, enough to, from the dance bar, you see. Was he better on trombone? Did he play? He was better on the trombone than he was on the cornet, but he could fill in, you see. Just like, like Wooden Joe, Wooden Joe could play cornet and then he'd fill it on the clarinet, too, you see.
